messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame stood in the doorway of the municipal decontamination lab, his fingers tracing the cold steel frame as he mapped the three possible exits before his foot even crossed the threshold. At sixty-two, he had spent the last decade living in the shadow of the pressure rupture that had split his life into before and after. Ten years earlier, he had been the lead bomb disposal technician when a pressurized chemical containment tank ruptured during a high-stakes field calibration. The shriek of the emergency sirens had split the air, followed by a hissing cloud of corrosive vapor that stung his lungs and burned his eyes. Medics had dragged him to the regional trauma center, where the sharp, clinical tang of industrial antiseptic had flooded his sinuses, sealing the memory of the chemical burn to his skin. He had survived the exposure, but the event had permanently rewired his perception of safety, turning every ordinary facility into a potential kill zone. He had come to believe that a single missed alarm meant death, a conviction that left no room for hesitation in his current work. In the months that followed, the laboratory never felt neutral again. When the automated warning klaxon from the fire suppression system blared during a routine inspection, his breath hitched and his body automatically shifted into a retreat posture, pushing him to abandon the floor and retreat to the breakroom, where he began insisting on keeping the door propped open. The sensory alarm directly catalyzed his need to avoid enclosed spaces and fueled his compulsion to pile on extra calibration shifts, ensuring his hands were never idle long enough to sit with the memory of the burning air. At the same time, the initial trigger of the siren immediately drove his physiological alarm system into overdrive, pulling his gaze across the room for the quickest path out before his conscious mind could even process the drill. Because his nervous system remained locked in this state of relentless threat monitoring, the ordinary whine of the facility’s HVAC equipment began to register as the precursor to another catastrophic rupture, sharpening his focus on environmental hazards until they felt indistinguishable from the original breach. This feedback loop tightened over the years, becoming the structural core of his daily survival. By refusing to sit in a room unaccompanied and by overworking himself to the point of exhaustion, he drained the psychological reserves needed to calm his own autonomic nerves, which in turn kept his startle reflex constantly primed to snap at the slightest unexpected contact. His wife learned to tap his shoulder only after announcing her presence, and he caught himself scanning the checkout aisles at the grocery store for the nearest doorway just to feel a fraction of control. The avoidance of medical cues became so absolute that he declined routine physicals, fearing the scratch of the blood pressure cuff would trigger a full respiratory shutdown. The constant scanning meant he never truly rested, and the unrelenting anticipation of disaster ensured that every ordinary workplace sound was instantly filtered through the lens of the original exposure. His supervisor noticed the tremor in his hands during precision wire cuts, eventually reassigning him to desk logistics, a demotion he interpreted as proof that his body had betrayed him. When a routine equipment test last month produced a sharp metallic ping, he dropped the calibration tablet, his heart hammering so violently he could not breathe, and finally called the clinic himself. He was terrified that without intervention, he would either lose his grip on his career entirely or suffocate in his own mind, and he hoped desperately to find a way to stand in a room without measuring the distance to the door.
